title: My dog ate something it shouldn't. What do I do now?
dek: Chocolate, grapes, a dropped pill, half a sock. Here's what to do in the first few minutes, and what not to do.
description: Dog ate chocolate, grapes, pills or a sock? What to do in the first minutes, who to call, what not to do, and the hidden dangers in yards and on trails.

glance.label: Before you try to make your dog throw up

body.title: If your dog is acting sick right now
body.text: Stop reading. If your dog is having trouble breathing, collapsing, shaking or having a seizure, go to the nearest emergency vet now and call them on the way.

children.text: It always happens fast. You turn around and the brownie plate is empty, or there's a chewed pill bottle on the floor, or your dog looks very proud of whatever they just found on the trail. Your stomach drops, and you grab your phone.

That's what this guide is for. It won't replace a vet, but it will help you make the right call quickly. With most poisonings, how fast you act decides how sick your dog gets, and how big the bill ends up being.
What to do in the next 10 minutes
Get your dog away from it.
Pick up whatever's left, and keep the wrapper, package or pill bottle. You'll need it.
Work out what, how much, and when.
Your best guess is fine. "About half a bar of dark chocolate, around 8pm" is exactly the kind of answer that helps.
Know your dog's weight.
The same amount can be nothing for a 70-pound Lab and dangerous for a 10-pound Chihuahua.
Call before you do anything else.
Your vet, the nearest emergency vet, or a pet poison hotline. They'll tell you whether to watch at home or come in now.
Don't wait for symptoms.
Many poisons look like nothing for hours, then cause damage that's harder and more expensive to treat.

body.title: Save these two numbers today
body.text:
[ASPCA Animal Poison Control: (888) 426-4435](tel:+18884264435)
[Pet Poison Helpline: (855) 764-7661](tel:+18557647661)

Both are open 24/7 and staffed by people who do nothing but animal poisonings. Both charge a one-time fee per case, usually under $100, and your vet can call them about the same case. Outside the US and Canada, call your vet or nearest emergency vet.

children.text: Is the fee worth it? Often, yes. If they tell you it's safe to watch at home, you may have just skipped an emergency visit. If they tell you to go in, your vet gets a plan from poison specialists, which helps them treat your dog faster.
Should I make my dog throw up?

Not on your own. This is the most common mistake owners make, and it comes from a good place. Making a dog vomit can help, but only for some things, only within a short window (usually a couple of hours), and only for some dogs.
Preventive Vet's guide
lists the cases where it does more harm than good.

For other things, it makes it worse. Sharp objects, batteries, cleaning products and fuels like gasoline can do more damage coming back up. A dog that's drowsy, shaky or struggling to breathe can inhale vomit into their lungs. Flat-faced breeds like Bulldogs and Pugs are at higher risk too.

And skip the old home remedies. Salt, mustard, milk and oil don't work well, and salt can poison a dog on its own. If a vet or poison line tells you to use hydrogen peroxide at home, they'll tell you exactly how much. Otherwise, let the clinic do it. They have medicine that works faster, and they can handle it if something goes wrong.

body.title: Even if your dog throws up
body.text: Vomiting doesn't mean it all came out. Call anyway. Some dogs still need treatment afterward.

children.text: The usual suspects, and how worried to be
Most poison calls come down to the same short list. According to
the ASPCA's poison control center
, over-the-counter medicines, everyday foods and chocolate are the top three reasons people call about their pets.

cells: Chocolate
Contains theobromine, which affects the heart and nervous system. Baking chocolate and cocoa powder are the worst. White chocolate has very little.
Call now. Signs can take hours to show up.
Grapes, raisins, currants
Can cause [kidney failure](https://www.aspcapro.org/node/104073). There's no known safe amount, and some dogs react to just a few.
Go in now, even if your dog seems fine.
Xylitol (sugar-free gum, mints, some peanut butters)
[Drops blood sugar fast](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/toxicology/food-hazards/xylitol-toxicosis-in-dogs) and can damage the liver.
Go in now. Signs can start within 30 minutes.
Human medicines (ibuprofen, naproxen, acetaminophen, ADHD and antidepressant pills)
Can harm the stomach, kidneys or liver, or overstimulate the heart and brain. One pill can be enough for a small dog.
Call now, with the bottle in your hand.
Onions, garlic, chives
Damage red blood cells. Signs may not show up for days.
Call. Large amounts and small dogs are the biggest worry.
Rat and mouse poison
Different products work in very different ways. Some cause bleeding days later.
Go in now, and bring the package.
Socks, toys, corn cobs, bones
Can get stuck in the stomach or intestines. Cooked bones can splinter.
Call. Watch for vomiting, not eating, or belly pain.

children.text: This isn't every poison, and it isn't a diagnosis. If what your dog ate isn't here, call anyway. It's what the hotlines are for.
The ones people don't think of
Most lists stop at chocolate and grapes. These four are easy to miss, because they're in yards, gardens and on trails instead of the kitchen.
Cannabis edibles
Where cannabis is legal, vets are seeing a lot more dogs who got into it, usually edibles.
Signs often start within an hour

: stumbling, dribbling pee, big pupils, and flinching at sounds or movement. Most dogs recover in a day or two with care, but edibles often contain chocolate or xylitol too, which can be the bigger problem.
Tell your vet exactly what it was. They aren't there to judge you, and there's no reliable quick test for it in dogs, so what you tell them shapes the treatment.
Snail and slug bait
Some snail and slug baits contain metaldehyde, which dogs seem to like the taste of. It causes tremors that can turn into seizures and dangerous overheating, and
a small amount is enough
. If you use snail bait, check the label for metaldehyde, and keep any bait where your dog can't reach it.
Sago palms
These spiky, palm-like plants are popular in warm-climate yards and as houseplants. Every part is toxic, especially the seeds, and it can cause liver failure.
The ASPCA says
up to half of cases are fatal, so any chewing on one is an emergency.
Wild mushrooms

After rain, mushrooms pop up in yards, parks and on trails. The death cap, which has spread far beyond its native Europe and often grows under oaks, can cause fatal liver failure, and it doesn't take much. You can't tell a safe mushroom from a dangerous one by looking, and neither can most of us. If your dog ate any wild mushroom, snap a photo or bring a piece in a paper bag, and call.
And if your walks go through dry grass, read our guide to
foxtails
. They're not a poison, but they send a lot of dogs to the vet.
What it might cost

Honest answer: it depends on what your dog ate and how fast they get help. A poison line call has its one-time fee. An emergency visit has a fee just to be seen, and treatment comes on top of that: medicine to make your dog vomit, activated charcoal, bloodwork, IV fluids, or a night or more in the hospital. We break down
what an emergency vet visit costs
, and you can always ask for an estimate with a low and high end before treatment starts.
The pattern is the same almost every time: early is cheaper than late. Making a dog vomit an hour after they ate grapes is a short visit. Treating kidney failure three days later is a hospital stay.
How to make your home safer
Keep purses, backpacks and coats off the floor. They're full of gum, mints and medicine.
Keep pills in a cabinet, not on the counter or nightstand. A pill organizer is easy for a dog to crack open.
Put the trash behind a door, or get a can with a locking lid.
Read labels for xylitol. It's sometimes listed as "birch sugar."
Be extra careful at holidays and parties, when there's food everywhere and guests don't know the rules.
Save a poison hotline number and your nearest 24-hour emergency vet in your phone.
Common questions

items.q: My dog ate chocolate but seems fine. Can I just watch them?
items.a: Maybe, but call first. Whether it's dangerous depends on the kind of chocolate, how much, and your dog's weight. Signs can take hours to show up, so "seems fine" right after doesn't tell you much.

items.q: How long until my dog shows signs?
items.a: It depends on what they ate. Xylitol can cause problems within 30 minutes. Chocolate often takes several hours. Grapes, onions, some rat poisons and toxic mushrooms can take a day or more. That's why calling early matters.
No. Vets see this every day, and it happens to careful owners too. The more honest you are about what happened, the better they can help.
Many accident and illness plans do, as long as nothing in your policy excludes it. It's worth checking yours before you ever need it.

children.text: If you're reading this after the scare and your dog is OK, take two minutes now. Save the numbers, look up your nearest emergency vet, and move the trash can. It's the kind of thing you only have to set up once.

title: Foxtails and dogs: the grass seed that sends dogs to the vet
dek: They look like harmless dry grass. But these little seeds can work their way into your dog's nose, ears or paws, and they only move one direction: in.
description: Foxtails are grass seeds that burrow into dogs' noses, ears and paws. How to spot one, when to see a vet, and how to keep them off your dog.

glance.label: Check paws, ears and coat in season

children.text: If you walk a dog anywhere with dry grass, ask your vet about foxtails and watch their face. These grass seeds are one of the most common reasons an otherwise healthy dog ends up at the vet in summer, and every so often they end up somewhere much deeper than a paw.
The good news is that foxtails are mostly preventable. And when one does get in, it's easiest to deal with, and cheapest, when you catch it early.
What a foxtail actually is
"Foxtail" isn't one plant. It's the nickname for the seed heads of several wild grasses, like wild barley, cheatgrass and
ripgut brome
, that grow in many parts of the world: along sidewalks, in empty lots, on trails and in backyards. Each seed has a sharp tip and tiny barbs that point backward.

Those barbs are the whole problem. Like a fishhook, a foxtail can move forward but not back. Every step, sniff and head shake can push it a little deeper. Left alone, one can work its way under the skin, and in rare cases into the lungs, spine or brain.
UC Davis vets have described
a foxtail that was breathed into a dog's lung, and another that worked its way from a hip wound toward the aorta, the body's main artery.
When foxtail season is

It depends on where you live, but the pattern is the same everywhere. While the grasses are green and soft, they're mostly harmless. As they dry out, the seed heads turn tan, get brittle and break apart, and that's when they start hitching rides on dogs.
In places with wet winters and dry summers, that's a long season. At
UC Davis's veterinary hospital

in California, foxtail cases usually start around April and taper off by fall, and in a warm, dry year they can turn up in any month. In cooler, wetter places the season tends to be shorter and later.
A simple rule: if the grass is dry and golden, assume it's full of foxtails.
Where they hide, and the signs

cells: Nose
Sudden, hard sneezing, pawing at the face, sometimes a bloody nose on one side
Ears
Head shaking, tilting the head, scratching at one ear
Eyes
Squinting, redness, goopy discharge, keeping one eye shut
Paws
Licking one spot between the toes, a small bump or swelling, limping
Mouth and throat
Gagging, coughing, trouble eating
Skin and private areas
A swelling or small hole that keeps draining, nonstop licking in one spot

children.text: Most of these start right after a walk. If your dog runs through dry grass and then starts sneezing hard or shaking their head, it's a foxtail until proven otherwise.
What to do if you think your dog has one
If you can see it sitting on the fur, or barely caught in the skin, you can gently pull it out with tweezers. Then keep an eye on that spot for a few days.

If it's in the nose, ear or eye, or already under the skin, don't go digging for it. Pulling can snap it and leave pieces behind, and the pieces keep moving. Don't put drops in the ear either. Call your vet and try to get in that day.

body.title: Why sooner is better
body.text: A foxtail near the surface can be a quick removal. One that's had days to travel can mean sedation, imaging and sometimes surgery. Early is easier on your dog and on your wallet.

children.text: Costs vary a lot. A foxtail your vet can grab during an exam may cost little more than the visit. Noses and ears often need sedation or anesthesia so the vet can see deep inside, which adds to the bill. The rare foxtail that travels into the chest or belly can mean scans and surgery that run into the thousands.
One pet insurance guide
puts the full range at under $100 to more than $5,000.
How to keep foxtails off your dog
Do a foxtail check after every walk in season.
Paws and between the toes, ears, armpits, under the tail and around the face. Run your hands against the fur, not just with it.
Skip the dry, tall grass.
Stick to paved paths and cleared trails, and keep your dog out of empty lots and field edges.
Keep the fur short where it counts.
Trimming between the toes and around the ears gives foxtails less to grab. Long-haired and curly-coated dogs pick up the most.
Clear them from your yard while they're green.
Pull or cut the grass before the seed heads dry. Mowing dry foxtails just scatters the seeds, as
Whole Dog Journal
points out. If they've already dried, bag them carefully.
Think about a mesh face guard for hikes.
Mesh hoods made for this cover the nose, ears and eyes. Some dogs pant more in them on hot days, so only use one while you're watching.
Common questions

items.q: Can a dog sneeze a foxtail out?
items.a: Sometimes. If the sneezing stops completely within a few minutes and doesn't come back, it may have come out. If it keeps going, comes back later, or there's blood, see your vet.

items.q: Are foxtails only a problem in the countryside?
items.a: No. They grow in cities too: in sidewalk cracks, median strips, vacant lots and overgrown yards. Plenty of foxtail cases start on an ordinary neighborhood walk.

items.q: My dog's paw is swollen but I can't see anything. Could it be a foxtail?
items.a: It could. Once one is under the skin, it's often invisible. A swelling between the toes that your dog keeps licking, especially after a walk through dry grass, is worth a vet visit.

Usually it's a same-day or next-day vet visit, not a wait-and-see. Go to an emergency vet if your dog has trouble breathing, won't stop sneezing and is bleeding a lot, or seems very tired and unwell after a hike.

children.text: Foxtails are one of those things nobody warns you about until it happens. Now you know. Check the paws, skip the dry grass, and the next time your dog sneezes like crazy after a walk, you'll know exactly what to look for.
